newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: GOLF-ELS WINS CLASSIC AFTER LONG CALLS PENALTY ON HIMSELF.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ELS WINS CLASSIC AFTER LONG CALLS PENALTY ON HIMSELF.

text.p: South African Ernie Els won the opening tournament of the European season by one shot on Sunday after his nearest rival effectively ruled himself out of contention for a rule infringement.
Els fired a final round 69 for a 10 under par aggregate of 278 to capture the (US$1.1 million) Johnnie Walker Classic from New Zealander Michael Long and Australian Peter Lonard.
Els completed his 18th tournament victory in atrocious conditions at the Hope Island resort course after torrential rain and lightning forced a one-hour interruption in mid-afternoon.

Long, who shared a two-shot overnight lead on nine under with Lonard and Australian Anthony Painter, was penalised one shot when he informed officials that his ball had moved as he lined up a putt on the 15th green.

Instead of putting for birdie and a possible share of the lead at the next tee, Long was faced with a 10 metre putt to save his par four. The ball shaved the hole for a bogey five, giving Els a crucial two-shot cushion.
Els, the 1994 U.S. Open champion and world number four, dropped a shot on the last hole in an unconvincing finish after taking the lead at the turn on a the final day.
"I got away with this one. ," Els told reporters. "In the future I think I will have to play a lot better than that coming down the stretch.

"I played some good golf for 13 holes and I had a chance to break away but then I lost it a bit. I am very relieved to have won, especially as I thought I would need a 66 to take it" said Els, who came from two shots off the pace overnight.
Els praised Long for his sportsmanship after calling the penalty on himself.
"No-one would have seen the ball move but Michael himself. Golf is a gentleman's game. It was quite a turnaround because I was not playing all that well at that stage."
Long, who, like Lonard, shot a level par 72 on Sunday, said the ball rolled back half a circumference after he addressed the ball.
"I did not dwell on it and I'm pleased that I held my game together over the last few holes to come so close," he said.
Englishman Nick Faldo, American Fred Couples and Painter shared fourth place on six under par.
Both Faldo and Couples, who were paired together, saw their hopes disappear at the par five 11th, where both players took double bogey sevens.
Faldo fluffed two approach shots as he took five strokes to get down from 50 metres from the pin while Couples hooked his tee shot into a lake.
"I just mis-hit the ball twice and that proved to be the end of it. I was out of contention from then on," Faldo, the U.S. Masters champion said.
Couples said: "I put it in the water and it was hard to believe that both of us would take seven. I was in it until then."
